summary: Defines CAPWAP, a protocol for centrally controlling and provisioning wireless access points through an Access Controller. It is designed to work with many wireless technologies, with separate binding documents for each. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: CAPWAP defines how a central Access Controller (AC) manages Wireless Termination Points (WTPs), the devices that connect wireless stations to a wired network. A WTP can discover an AC, establish a protected control connection, receive settings and send wireless traffic through it. Separate bindings adapt CAPWAP to different wireless technologies.

subtitle: How a controller discovers, secures and configures wireless access points over IP.

tldr.problem: Wireless access points were often configured by hand or through proprietary methods. RFC 5415 defines a shared protocol for a controller to manage them over an IP network.
tldr.mechanism: A Wireless Termination Point (WTP) discovers an Access Controller (AC), establishes a DTLS-protected control connection, joins, and receives configuration. CAPWAP also carries wireless frames between the WTP and AC when the selected mode tunnels them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5415 defines a technology-neutral base protocol with separate bindings for specific wireless technologies. It is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5415 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009, and the unit metadata says RFC 8553 and RFC 8996 update it. Its IEEE 802.11 binding is specified separately in RFC 5416.

sections.title: Why CAPWAP Centralizes Wireless Management
sections.content:
RFC 5415 defines the Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) protocol. It lets an Access Controller (AC) manage Wireless Termination Points (WTPs), which connect wireless stations to a wired network. The protocol carries communication between a WTP and an AC over IP.

The RFC describes earlier management as manual configuration, proprietary Layer 2 methods, or no central management. CAPWAP aims to centralize authentication and policy, move higher-level processing away from cost-constrained WTPs, and support multiple wireless technologies. Communication between ACs and between a station and an AC are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: CAPWAP gives a central Access Controller (AC) a standard way to manage Wireless Termination Points (WTPs). A WTP is a device that connects wireless stations to a wired network. The protocol covers the link between a WTP and an AC, not communication between controllers or between a station and a controller.

sections.title: Two Ways to Handle Wireless Frames
sections.content:
CAPWAP has a Split MAC mode and a Local MAC mode. In Split MAC, the WTP encapsulates wireless data and management frames and sends them to the AC. In Local MAC, the WTP processes wireless management frames itself; it can bridge data frames locally or send them to the AC as IEEE 802.3 frames.

The base protocol does not define the radio-specific details. Each wireless technology uses a binding, a companion specification that supplies its message elements and payload rules. A binding must define radio information, station configuration information and statistics. The IEEE 802.11 binding is specified in RFC 5416.
sections.plainLanguage: CAPWAP lets the WTP and AC divide wireless work in two ways. Split MAC sends wireless data and management frames to the AC; Local MAC has the WTP handle management frames and may keep data frames local. Each radio technology needs its own binding, which defines the details the base protocol leaves open.

sections.title: Finding an AC and Starting a Session
sections.content:
Discovery is optional. A WTP with an AC address already configured can skip it; otherwise, it sends a Discovery Request and considers the Discovery Responses from available ACs. The WTP chooses an AC and starts a Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) handshake. The handshake uses a cookie exchange before the peers complete authentication and establish the secure session.

After DTLS is established, the WTP sends a Join Request and the AC responds. The WTP and AC exchange configuration messages, and the WTP reports the result of applying the configuration. They then enter the Run state, where the WTP periodically sends Echo Requests when other control traffic does not keep the connection active.
sections.plainLanguage: A WTP can use a preconfigured AC or discover one by sending a request and collecting replies. It then uses Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) to establish a protected session with the chosen AC. The WTP asks to join, exchanges settings with the AC, and enters service after reporting its configuration state.

sections.title: The Session Moves Through Defined States
sections.content:
CAPWAP defines one lifecycle state machine for both the AC and WTP. It governs which messages are valid at each stage and coordinates with DTLS through commands and notifications. A WTP has one state-machine instance because it communicates with one AC; the AC maintains state for each WTP session and separate handling for discovery.

The path includes discovery, DTLS setup and authorization, joining, configuration, and Run. A WTP may enter Image Data to obtain firmware before configuration is complete. Repeated discovery or DTLS failures can put it in Sulking, where it waits for the SilentInterval before trying again. Reset and DTLS teardown end or restart a session.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol allows only certain messages at each point in a session. A WTP discovers or selects an AC, establishes DTLS, joins, receives settings and then reaches Run. After repeated connection failures, it waits before trying discovery again.

sections.title: Transport, Discovery and Message Size
sections.content:
The WTP acts as a UDP client and the AC listens as a server. The AC uses UDP port 5246 for control and 5247 for data; the WTP may choose its own ports. IPv4 CAPWAP packets set the UDP checksum field to zero. Over IPv6, the control channel uses UDP and the data channel defaults to UDP-Lite unless a middlebox or IPv4-to-IPv6 gateway has been discovered.

A WTP can send discovery to a broadcast address, the CAPWAP multicast address, or a known AC address. CAPWAP also fragments its own messages because firewalls and network address translation (NAT) devices may discard IP fragments. Fragment identifiers can wrap and cause pieces of different messages to be confused, so the RFC recommends path MTU discovery. Every implementation must receive a reassembled message of at least 4096 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: CAPWAP separates control messages from wireless data and sends them to different AC ports. A WTP can find a controller by broadcast, multicast or a known address. CAPWAP can split large messages into pieces, but the RFC warns that its fragment identifiers can wrap, so implementations should discover the path size and avoid fragmentation when possible.

sections.title: Headers Mark the Packet Type and Payload
sections.content:
CAPWAP packets share a transport header that identifies the version, radio, wireless binding and payload format. Its flags indicate whether the packet is fragmented, whether it is the final fragment, and whether optional radio information is present. The header also carries a fragment identifier and offset so the receiver can reassemble the payload.

Control packets carry a control header followed by message elements. Data packets carry an encapsulated wireless frame, either in the native format defined by its binding or as an IEEE 802.3 frame. Discovery Request and Response control messages are sent without DTLS; every other control message must be protected by DTLS. The AC policy determines whether data packets use DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The CAPWAP header tells the receiver which radio and wireless format a packet uses, and whether it is part of a fragmented message. Control packets carry instructions and settings; data packets carry wireless frames. DTLS protects all control messages except discovery, while the AC decides whether to protect data packets.

sections.title: Control Requests Are Reliable and Ordered
sections.content:
Control messages use request and response pairs. Each carries a sequence number, which lets the sender match a response to its request. A request's message elements use a type-length-value format, so each element identifies its type and length before its contents. CAPWAP assigns odd message types to requests and the next even type to the matching response.

Only one request may be outstanding at a time. If the response does not arrive, the sender retransmits the same request with increasing delays. The receiver caches the last response and sends it again for a duplicate request, without processing the request a second time; it ignores older requests. The AC and WTP can also exchange station settings, events, statistics and configuration updates through these control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Every control request has a matching response and a sequence number that pairs them. If a response is lost, the sender retries the same request after a longer wait. The receiver can recognize a retry and resend its saved response without repeating the requested action.

sections.title: Configuration and Firmware Updates
sections.content:
A WTP may keep no configuration and accept the AC's settings, or save non-default settings locally. When it saves settings, it reports its overrides to the AC during configuration, and the AC replies with its settings. The AC keeps a copy of each active WTP's configuration; if the WTP joins another AC after a failure, it can provide its overrides to that AC. The AC can also change settings while the WTP is in Run.

Firmware management is optional. The AC can name the firmware the WTP should run during joining. If the WTP does not have that image, the devices exchange Image Data messages; if the WTP already has it, it can reset to use it. A download started during Run can happen while the WTP continues serving clients, and the WTP waits for a Reset Request before restarting. The protocol does not verify that the WTP reports its firmware version truthfully or stores the image correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The AC sends settings to the WTP and keeps a copy of active WTP configuration. A WTP can report its saved changes if it connects to a different AC. Firmware can be downloaded while the WTP is serving clients, but the protocol does not check whether the device stores or reports the image correctly.

sections.title: Security and Operational Limits
sections.content:
DTLS protects the control connection and can also protect the data channel. Peers authenticate with certificates or pre-shared keys; the RFC strongly discourages pre-shared keys and recommends unique keys rather than reused or memorable passphrases. Certificates must distinguish ACs from WTPs, and both devices must authorize their peer. Discovery is sent in the clear, so an AC must not discard an active session merely because it receives a Discovery Request.

The RFC also identifies limits. An unprotected data channel can expose its Session ID and allow forged data traffic. An attacker may delete protected records and force a session restart, and CAPWAP specifies no congestion control for its data channel. The RFC recommends against tunneling traffic that has no congestion control. It also advises using CAPWAP as the WTP's configuration interface so that the AC's stored state does not become inconsistent with the device.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects CAPWAP control traffic, and it can protect data traffic when the AC requires it. The RFC warns that clear discovery messages must not be treated as proof that a device restarted, and that an unprotected data channel has security limits. CAPWAP also defines no congestion control for that channel, so the RFC recommends against sending traffic that has no congestion control through it.

fields.desc: Version and type of the following header.

fields.name: RID
fields.desc: Radio ID; values range from 1 to 31.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Selects native wireless or 802.3 frame format.

fields.name: W
fields.desc: Marks the optional wireless-specific information field.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Marks the optional radio MAC address field.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved bits; senders set them to zero.

fields.name: Fragment Offset
fields.desc: Fragment position in units of eight octets.

fields.desc: Reserved bits; senders set them to zero.
